entry.title: Can We Make Digital Consciousness?
entry.content:
Okay, so we already have neural networks and we’re getting pretty good at making them. They’re essentially massive quilts of nodes passing signals to each other and modifying themselves when it’s suitable to do so. Like airplanes modeled after birds, camera lenses after our irises and wind turbines after whale flippers, we’ve modeled our digital brains after our human ones.

Because ultimately, our brains are just a bunch of neurons that pass signals to each other, and which modify themselves when it’s suitable to do so.

So: if we had limitless funding, energy and researchers to combine an unfathomable 86 billion digital neurons into one machine, could we just… make a brain?

In fact, is that all our brains are? We have a few different types of neurons, broadly categorized under sensory, motor, and interneurons. But they really just function the same: They accept a range of inputs from neighboring neurons though dendrites, process them in a nucleus, and send outputs via an axon. Instead of digital signals, neurons play telephone using chemical neurotransmitters. Regardless of the medium, all neurons are are inputs, a weight, and an output. NIH

In fact, the parallels between our understanding of digital systems and our own brains even bleed into the language neuroscientists use to describe how our brain works:

Roland

It’s a rather bleak image of what it means to be human; a body controlled by chain reactions that break down the soul into bits and bytes, each cell acting on repetition and reaction based on its immediate surroundings, unaware of any meaning or purpose. It, I said. Are we just made of many, tiny, its?

Well, if there’s anything I learned from my AP Psychology class in high school, it’s that we know barely anything about how our bodies work.

Looking into it, it turns out that neurons might be the most diverse kinds of cells in the body, with hundreds of subtypes that send and receieve in different ways NIH. We don’t know if neurons communicate in chains, micro-circuits, or organized columns. A single neuron axon can have 1,000 branches that spread across the brain. Much of the processing in a neuron happens in the dendrites (the inputs), yet it still is rarely modeled at all in digital simulations. We have no idea how intrinsic activity in brains emerge—somehow, messy cellular noise across our brains across billions of neurons perfectly synchronize into massive, slow-moving waves that form dreams and deep thought and consume the vast majority of the brain’s energy. Roland

We don’t even know if our brains function using time as the independent variable. Of course, it’s the most convenient option to record brain activity spikes according to a stopwatch, which is what the majority of neuroscience bases its research on. But there’s experimental inconsistencies that suggest our neurons function based on spatial or state parameters. Time could very much be a subjective experience. In high-adrenaline situations, people report feeling like time slows down—it’s entirely possible that for them, time really does slow down. Roland

NOTE: I was going somewhere with this but my thoughts will have to be continued at a later date.

entry.title: The Energy AI Paradox
entry.content:
NOTE: This is not a finalized research paper. Its depth and factual precision will need to be refined. So take everything with a grain of salt.

Environmental Impacts of AI

A frequent criticism of generative AI is regarding the environmental impact of training and querying the models. They splurge on electricity grids, soak up drinking water, and strain local supplies. Data centers as a whole (of which modern AI is only a subset) have already surpassed using 1.5% of the world’s electricity generation, with estimates of global AI electricity consumption at 0.5%. In the realm of the U.S., AI accounts for about 2% of national electricity consumption. And in my lovely hometown of Northern Virginia, data centers take up over 25%. [OurWorldInData]

But like all technologies, the AI optimists argue, the innovation comes first and the optimizations come second. The IEA claims that just in the past couple years, basic queries have gotten so efficient that “if all conventional internet searches were performed with simple AI text queries, it would consume less than… 1% of total data centre consumption today.” Which is surprising, given that the general rule of thumb for vague environmentalists has been to avoid using ChatGPT when a simple google search would do (To be fair, I’m not certain if that estimation includes the initial training costs of the models). The problem is that along with the efficiency gains come a larger demand for higher-intensity applications—like video generation or reasoning—which can drastically boost electricity usage (see Jevons Paradox).

I’ve also recently been seeing arguments that AI can actually optimize the efficiency of the electricity grid and negate these negative effects long term. The IEA claims that up to 175 GW of transmission capacity could be unlocked without any new lines being built, which is more than the predictions of data center power load by 2030. And in the R&D field, AI seems to be a perfect fit for materials optimization in areas such as solar PV, where only 0.01% of next-gen materials have been tested.

So what’s really happening? Is AI bad for the environment or not? Perhaps it’s bad in the short term, but better for the long term?

Well, there’s a catch. A few catches, really.

The missing nuance lies underneath umbrella terms and misleading implications. All of these claims center around how much electricity is consumed by AI, and therefore how environmentally damaging it is. Once these 2 terms are broken down, they will reveal patterns that constantly distort discussions about AI.

AI is a Terrible Term

Firstly: AI is a terrible term (as I will probably continue to complain about in the future). Are we talking about our good ol’ ChatGPT, video game NPCs, optimization algorithms, Skynet, or video generators? These are all significantly different concepts. It doesn’t make sense to argue in support of LLM training in data centers on the basis that an optimization algorithm can improve power lines—it’s not like anyone’s planning to supercharge them with Grok! This goes the same for materials optimization for solar PV. But what about drug discovery? That’s a use case of AI that most people can get behind. Google’s AlphaFold achieved a revolutionary 45,000x acceleration in protein structure mapping using “AI” [BezosEarthFund]. Well, believe it or not, they’re not using a fork of Gemini underneath. While it does use a transformer-style neural network, it’s very much a separate entity to LLMs.

So, it’s crucial to stop using the blanket term “AI” and at the very least draw a distinction between general-purpose LLMs and specialized machine learning. One can argue in favor of LLMs, but should not conflate it with algorithms that can actually optimize research and power usage.

And here’s the thing: you can probably guess how much data centers are used to train LLMs compared to specialized machine learning models. I’ll give you a hint: LLMs are trained on the entirety of the internet. Self-driving cars or power grid optimizers are not. LLM training operates on a scale multiple orders of magnitude larger than targeted AI. Therefore, most of the electricity going into AI training is not directly assisting with long-term energy reduction. The environmental benefits of specialized machine learning cannot be used to justify the environmental costs of general-purpose LLMs.

Not All Electricity Is Equal

Using electricity is not inherently bad. In fact, I would consider it good; it allows us to do a lot of cool stuff. The bigger concern is how electricity is produced. If data centers were all powered with solar panels and wind turbines, I doubt there would be as much concern for the environmental impact as there is today. So the implication that electricity usage = environmental damage is not necessarily correct. Rather, the environmental impact of electricity varies by carbon-intensity.

But first, quantifying how much electricity LLMs use up is very difficult. I’ll divide the electricity usage of LLMs into four stages: preparation, training, fine-tuning, and inference.

Patterns of AI computing load, from Arxiv.

The preparation stage, while not itself consuming significant electricity relative to the lifecycle, can have drastic effects on the efficiency of the training process (reductions of >90%!). Effectively, this stage centers around data acquisition (scraping the entire Internet) and optimizations come from filtering through redundancies or feature selection.

Training is the foundational, power-hungry process of building a model. It’s where tens of thousands of GPUs run for days or weeks straight, momentarily burdening the energy grid with the consumption similar to an entire town. It’s impossible for us commoners to know the exact energy consumption during model training of the most popular LLMs out there because none of them disclose it (you can imagine why).

The fine-tuning phase adapts a pre-trained model to tasks typically expected of an LLM through tweaks to the model.

Inference is what happens every time a query is run, and operates on a much smaller scale of power usage. However, because any given model experiences millions or billions of queries, the impact of inferences stack up to the training. For example, inference takes up 60% of AI energy usage at Google compared to 40% on training. Other estimates place inference at 90% of total lifecycle use [Arxiv].

from OurWorldInData.

Given that the majority of AI energy use comes from inference, this chart from OurWorldInData can be made based off of available estimates for individual queries. Comparatively, these estimates of AI energy usage seem minor compared to other daily activities.

Remember that quote from the IEA earlier? That if we used simple AI text queries instead of conventional searches we would use less than 1% of data center consumption? This chart shows why: basic queries are very efficient already. So we’re left with a very large gap between the energy consumption of basic queries and the total footprint of the AI industry. That gap is exactly where the tech bros and AI movie enthusiasts lie. Reasoning models and video generators can use potentially hundreds of times more energy than simple queries. So you don’t have to feel bad about Google automatically suggesting AI responses—but you might want to think twice about vibecoding a new project management SaaS.

Now we come back to the main problem: how this electricity is sourced. Firstly, these data centers require continuous upkeep, which inherently make intermittent renewable energy sources such as solar or wind less viable compared to stable energy sources like coal and gas. The carbon-intensity of electricity used by data centers is 48% higher than the US average. This is one reason why many have clumped together around coal-heavy grids such as Virginia, West Virginia and Pennsylvania. And while there are plans to build more nuclear facilities to substitute fossil fuels, they are unlikely to materialize with enough power to make a substantial difference in the next decade. [MIT Technology Review]

The second problem also stems from the clustering of data centers in specific cities: it places a local strain on the energy economy. The 5% of national electricity usage by data centers are not distributed equally throughout the U.S., but are instead drawing from highly localized areas, which can contribute to higher electricity costs from households (although there are several other significant factors involved in this—see Concrete Logic).

So, to recap from the electricity standpoint: the electricity used by AI occurs primarily during inference and relies on electricity with 50% more carbon footprint than the national average.

What This Means

The main takeaways that I’ve learned from this process are:

  • Simple LLM queries are very power efficient, but advanced reasoning models and video generators make up the bulk of power usage.
  • General-purpose LLMs require drastically more electricity to train than specialized machine learning.
  • Specialized machine learning is what enables drug discovery and power grid optimization innovations, not LLMs.
  • The environmental benefits of specialized machine learning cannot be used to justify the environmental costs of LLMs.
  • Model inference takes up significantly more lifecycle energy use than training.
  • Data centers/AI use electricity that is 50% more carbon-intense.
  • Data centers centralize power consumption in highly localized areas.

I’m sure that there are plenty of aspects I haven’t yet considered related to energy and AI (and I haven’t even touched any of the other environmental or societal impacts), but this has already helped me realize how much misleading information exists just because of unclear terminology.

entry.title: The Indie Web Rabbit Hole
entry.content:
It’s day 2 of my website redesign and I’m already overwhelmed by the lingo.

That’s not to say it hasn’t been going well. I’ve been switching between poking around Neocities sites and piecing together my own, building up a design language and workflow for CSS art.

My own little collection of blinkies.

So, to sum it up: there’s this whole movement that’s been going on for the past decade or so called the Indie Web—a pushback against the corporate web through the forms of personal, off-the-grid, anti-algorithm websites symbolized by that zany retro 90s aesthetic of the early internet. It’s simultaneously self-aware of the current state of social media and, for lack of a better word, role-playing as living in that era. It treats websites as digital bedrooms, usually being decorated with the web-equivalent of posters, bookshelves, and sticky notes that say what the owner is up to. Contrary to what I had been mostly designing before, these websurfers aren’t building a portfolio. They’re not trying to sell anything to anyone. They’re collecting experiences from the internet—books, websites, gifs, movies, trends, art—and decorating a corner to be themselves in.

These netizens share around “blinkies”—little 88x31 gifs—like eccentric jokes; there are some archives of them, like on thuvien.org, but they’re usually found by browsing other indie websites and accumulating them over time. Of course, they’re not to be confused with “buttons,” “badges,” or “stamps,” which I’m sure have some nuanced difference between each other. There are also “webshrines,” which are highly curated pages devoted to specific pieces of art or media (altalenae has a good one for Arrival), and which I can very much see doing for Ian Hubert or Hawaii Pt. II down the road.

Some other websites I’ve liked (which I do want to move to a node later on) are:

  • irony-machine
  • lazybones

As someone who treats Minecraft servers as third places, who has a soft spot for interactive text adventures, and who has had a building resentment of modern social media, I can absolutely feel myself falling in love with this treatment of the internet. I truly believe that everyone—at least, everyone who currently occupies themselves with social media—should have a personal site. It doesn’t have to display one’s deepest fears or love lives. But it importantly shifts the frame of viewing others lives away from glancing through windows past poster ads from a train seat and instead towards stepping inside someone’s home for a little bit and catching up over tea. On these sites, you’re not battling against an algorithm or the weighty momentum of your audience’s scrolling. And that’s important. To me, at least.

entry.title: Redesigning My Website
entry.content:
The current home page of my personal website.

My website is in a bit of an identity crisis.

It doesn’t know whether it’s a personal website or a professional one. It doesn’t know if it should be retro-stylized corner-of-the-internet or a sleek and minimalistic portfolio archive. If it should house refined essays and reflections or stream-of-consciousness ideas. And it certainly doesn’t know if it should be viewed on iPhones.

Today I want to redesign it to actually fit my needs. I won’t be able to finish everything—if anything, this website will constantly be evolved over time—but I at least want a structure that matches what comes out of my brain and what should go into others.

My website is rather unique in that I need to present the same parts of myself in different ways. For example, I built a 6-foot tall, 140 lb cat tower earlier this summer. Ultimately, it’s a personal passion project that I built for myself and my family and my first real venture into woodworking. But it also happens to be a portfolio piece for my mechanical engineering career—a concrete example of something I designed, priced, and constructed through sheer self-motivation. It’s one project, but there are two audiences: a friend or family spectator who might be interested in my life, or a potential employer who only has the time to skim what matters. And the gap between the two only widens when I get to discussing my development for my game Tracerouter or Blender projects. What things do I want my employers to see, or to not see? My friends and family? Members of the internet?

To start, I need a clearer separation of the content I share here. I’m planning on dividing it into 4 categories, which can be thought of as a range from evolving, time-independent pages to momentary blips of ideas:

  1. Nodes: Persistent, ever-evolving pages or hubs about topics or concepts from my life. Think: photo collections, my views on the energy industry, or my list of all-time favorite video games.
  2. Projects: Substantial things I’ve created or worked on, professional or not. The project may conclude, but the notes may continue to be refined.
  3. Writings: Essays, guides, or any other well-thought-out arrangements of words I’m confident enough to attach my name to.
  4. Journal: About as informal as it gets here on this site! From a couple sentences to a word wall, this are thoughts that are one layer about my actual handheld journal. This page counts as one.

Now, instead of having a uniform aesthetic that is mediocre at both expressing my personality for the more personal pages and being straight-to-the-point for potential employers, I’m planning on creating a wider range of styles that varies based on formality. The home page needs to have clear directions and an immediate understanding of my personality and capabilities. I’ve gotten inspired by websites on Neocities, such as altalenae’s, for how well they capture the feeling of the “indie web” and the eccentric and passionate persona they express.

The home page of altalenae, Em's website.

What I particularly like:

  • “Bookshelf” section, with favorite books, articles, and reviews.
  • “Currently” sections, such as what they’re currently reading, or doing.
  • Plenty of links on the home page with icons.

While I do really appreciate the retro aesthetic of all these Neocities websites, I’d prefer for my website to stand out in its own unique way. I’ve recently been looking into Russian Constructivism, in particular the architectural works of Yakov Chernikhov. I think it would be interesting to integrate the bold and geometrical style that still references an older time.

Iconic russian constructivist poster.

Taking after these styles, here’s a quick half-done mockup I’ve just made in Figma of what my home page could look like:



After spending some time learning how to make masks and geometric shapes with CSS, here is what I’ve come up with so far:

While it’s not fully fleshed out, I feel like it already comes off as a much more unique and interesting website. I designed the previous version of the home page nearly 2 years ago, and since then the oversized “Hi, I’m Haroon” header has aged like milk in the days of vibe-coded websites (even though I didn’t use AI for it). I already like the split down the middle that separates the white background—the more traditional colors and professional categories like “projects” and “engineering”—from the dark, more zany (I’m looking into the future, here) side of my website, with dithered photos and angled buttons. Once I detail this page with more links, widgets and shapes, I think this home page will stand out and present the 2 different, yet still coherent, sides of myself.
